Understand the pathophysiology of rotational ankle fractures.

surgical approaches, surgical fixation, and syndesmosis involvement.

Overview
The ankle is the most frequently injured weight-bearing joint.
Injury usually results from indirect rotational forces but less commonly results from a direct
blow; injury may result in fracture and ligamentous and soft-tissue injury.
Ankle stability depends on bony and ligamentous integrity; injury to both must be recognized
and managed.
Classified based on anatomic site, mechanism of injury
Danis-Weber classification is based on anatomic site and uses level of lateral malleolus
fracture in relation to articular surface.
Lauge-Hansen classification is based on mechanism of injury and predicts the position of
foot and the direction of primary deforming force based on displacement pattern, level, and
morphology of fibular fracture.
Individualize treatment decisions based on bony and ligamentous stability not classification
system.
Subluxation of talus within the ankle mortise commonly is present; even minimal mortise
malalignment alters contact pressures and risks arthritis.
It is imperative to achieve a stable, anatomically reduced mortise by restoring bony and
ligamentous structures.
Critical to assess the condition of the soft tissues
Marked swelling, fracture blisters, or other skin changes should delay definitive surgical
management until soft-tissue milieu improves. Open fractures require urgent irrigation and
débridement and provisional reduction.
Can wait as long as 3 weeks postinjury for definitive management
Condition of soft tissues particularly important in elderly patients and patients with diabetes
mellitus
Most nondisplaced or minimally displaced (<2 mm) isolated lateral malleolus fractures are
managed nonsurgically.
Isolated malleolus fractures displaced more than 2 mm, bimalleolar and trimalleolar fractures,
fracture-dislocations, syndesmotic injuries, and open fractures require surgical management.
The key factor is stability under the tibial plafond.
Historically, the recommendation was to reduce posterior malleolus fragments greater than
25% of the tibial plafond; recent literature suggests expanding indications for posterior
malleolus fixation, with greater focus on combined stability, including improved fibular
reduction and restored syndesmotic integrity.

Overview
The ankle is the most frequently injured weight-bearing joint in the body, making ankle
injuries common for most orthopaedic surgeons. Injury usually is the result of indirect
rotational forces and less commonly is from a direct blow. These forces result not only in
bone fracture but also variable degrees of soft-tissue and cartilage injury. Because ankle
stability depends on bone and ligament integrity, injury to both types of structures must
be recognized and managed appropriately1 (Resource 1).
Fractures may be classified based on the anatomic site of injury or the mechanism of
injury. The Lauge-Hansen classification system is the most common mechanistic type of
classification system. This classification system predicts the position of the foot and the
direction of the primary deforming force based on the displacement pattern, level, and
morphology of the fibular fracture. The most common anatomic classification system is
the Danis-Weber classification system. This system uses the level of the lateral malleolus
fracture in relation to the articular surface to classify these injuries.1
Similar to many classification systems, these classification systems do not perfectly
predict the need for surgical management. Each injury must be individualized, and
treatment decisions must be based on overall stability. Common to many of these
injuries is some degree of subluxation of the talus within the ankle mortise. Even
minimal mortise malalignment has long been believed to result in altered contact
pressures and a risk of subsequent arthritis; therefore, the goal in the successful
management of these injuries is a stable, anatomically reduced ankle mortise. Stability is
imparted by restoring bony anatomy and repairing/reconstructing injured ligaments.1
Proper management of the soft tissues is equally important. After closed reduction and
splinting, marked swelling, the presence of fracture blisters, or other skin changes
should delay surgical management until the soft-tissue milieu improves. A splint may
adequately stabilize a fracture while awaiting soft-tissue recovery; however, if gross
instability precludes adequate maintenance of reduction with the use of a splint, then an
external fixator can be used to maintain overall alignment while awaiting definitive

AP, mortise, and lateral radiographs should be obtained in patients in whom ankle

The importance of dynamic stress radiographs is a subject of debate. These views may
demonstrate dynamic talar shift that may be underappreciated on static, nonstress
radiographs. Similarly, injury to the syndesmosis may be obvious, with widening of the
distal tibiofibular joint, or visualized only on dynamic stress examination.1

Epidemiology
Rotational fractures of the ankle are among the most common injuries requiring orthopaedic
management.
Ankle fractures vary from relatively simple injuries with minimal long-term effects to complex
injuries with severe long-term sequelae.
Population-based studies have identified an increase in the incidence of ankle fractures.2,3
Data suggest the mean annual rate of ankle fractures in the United States is 4.2 fractures per

Rates of surgical management vary depending on the type of fracture.
For isolated lateral malleolus fractures, which account for two-thirds of rotational ankle
fractures, the surgical management rate is approximately 11%.
For fractures of the lateral, medial, and posterior fragments, the surgical management rate is
74%.
Risk factors for an ankle fracture include age, increased body mass, and a history of ankle
fracture.
The highest incidence of ankle fractures is in elderly women.

Epidemiology
Ankle fractures are among the most common of all fractures. The annual incidence has
been found to be 71 to 187 per 100,000 people. Fractures about the ankle range from a
malleolar avulsion fracture to a comminuted fracture of the articular surface, with a
resulting spectrum of stability and congruity of the mortise. A small incongruity in the
ankle may lead to changes in the pressure distribution of the joint surface, which may
then lead to an arthritic ankle. A 1-mm shift of the talus may result in a 40% loss of
contact area. The goal in the management of an ankle fracture should be to restore
congruity and stability to the ankle and to maintain it through the healing process5
(Resource 2).

Osteology
The osseous anatomy of the ankle provides stability during weight bearing and mobility in
plantar flexion.
The ankle is stabilized by the inherent bony configuration of the mortise, formed by the distal
tibia and fibula, and the medial and lateral ligament complexes.

Vascular Anatomy
The medial and lateral malleoli are supplied with terminal branches from the anterior tibial,
posterior tibial, and peroneal arteries.
Nerves

Nerves
Motor innervation to the superficial and deep posterior compartment muscles comes
primarily from the tibial nerve, whereas the anterior compartment muscles are
innervated by the deep peroneal nerve and the lateral compartment muscles are
innervated by the superficial peroneal nerve. Sensory innervation to the anterolateral
ankle comes from the superficial peroneal nerve, the posterolateral ankle from the sural
nerve, and the medial ankle from the saphenous nerve.
Tendons
Posterior group
The posterior group includes the Achilles and plantaris tendons.
The sural nerve is immediately lateral to the Achilles tendon.
Medial group
On the medial side of the ankle, the flexor tendons, including the tibialis posterior, the flexor
digitorum longus, and the flexor hallucis longus, course posterior to the medial malleolus.
The posterior tibial artery and the tibial nerve lie between the flexor digitorum longus and
flexor hallucis longus tendons.
The saphenous vein and nerve course superior and anterior to the tip of the medial
malleolus and are at risk during surgical repair of medial malleolus fractures.
Anterior group
On the anterior aspect of the ankle, the extensor retinaculum contains the extensor tendons,
including the tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, and
peroneus tertius.
Between the extensor hallucis longus and the extensor digitorum longus lie the deep
peroneal nerve and the anterior tibial artery.

The superficial peroneal nerve crosses the ankle anterior to the lateral malleolus, superficial
to the extensor retinaculum.
Because the superficial peroneal nerve may cross from the lateral compartment to the
anterior compartment at varying levels, care must be exercised to avoid injury to this nerve
in the management of fibular fractures.
Lateral group
On the lateral side of the ankle, the peroneal tendons are contained by a stout retinacular
structure posterior to the fibula.
The peroneus longus is more external and posterior to the peroneus brevis.
Lateral approaches to the ankle can injure the superficial peroneal nerve more proximally
and the sural nerve more distally.

Tendons
The posterior group muscles largely serve to plantarflex the ankle. The medial group
muscles includes the flexors of the toes. The posterior tibialis tendon adducts and
inverts and acts as a plantar flexor in some positions. Anterior group muscles include the
tibialis anterior, which dorsiflexes the ankle and inverts the foot; the peroneus tertius, a
weak dorsi flexor and evertor; and the toe extensors, which serve as secondary
dorsiflexors. Lastly, the lateral group tendons are ankle evertors and are dynamic
stabilizers of the ankle, which is especially important in patients with lateral ligament
insufficiency.
Joints and Ligaments
The ankle joint behaves like a true mortise in dorsiflexion.
Stability is achieved by articular contact between the medial malleolus, fibula, tibial plafond,
and talus.
The talar dome is wider anteriorly than posteriorly so that, as the ankle dorsiflexes, the fibula
rotates externally through the tibiofibular syndesmosis to accommodate the talus.6
The lateral malleolus is surrounded by multiple strong ligaments.

These include the interosseous membrane and the tibiofibular ligamentous complex,
consisting of the interosseous ligament and the syndesmotic ligaments (anterior inferior
tibiofibular ligament [AITFL], posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament, inferior transverse
tibiofibular ligament, inferior interosseous ligament).
These ligaments are responsible for the stability of the ankle in external rotation.
In addition, the lateral collateral ligaments of the ankle, including the anterior and posterior
talofibular ligaments and the calcaneofibular ligaments, provide support and resistance to
inversion and anterior translation of the talus relative to the fibula.
Medial malleolus
The medial malleolus surface of the distal tibia has a larger surface anteriorly than
posteriorly.
The posterior border of the medial malleolus includes the groove for the posterior tibial
tendon.
The medial malleolus includes the anterior malleolus, which is larger than and extends
approximately 0.5 cm distal to the posterior malleolus.
The deltoid ligament provides medial ligamentous support of the ankle.
The deep component of the deltoid ligament arises from the intercollicular groove and the
posterior malleolus. It is a short, thick ligament inserting on the medial surface of the talus.
The superficial deltoid ligament arises from the anterior malleolus of the medial malleolus
and inserts into the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus
The orientation of both ligaments is primarily vertical with respect to the ground.

Joints and Ligaments
The body of the talus resides in a bony mortise created by the articulation between the
distal fibula and tibia. The mortise is formed by the tibial plafond and the medial and
lateral malleoli. Composed of the talus, distal tibia, and fibula, the ankle joint includes
three articulations: tibiofibular, tibiotalar, and talofibular. The tibiofibular joint
represents the inferior extent of the lower extremity syndesmosis. The syndesmosis is
stabilized by four ligaments: the AITFL, posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament, transverse
tibiofibular ligament, and interosseous tibiofibular ligament3 (Resource 3).

The ankle is stabilized by the inherent bony configuration of the mortise and the medial
and lateral ligament complexes. With the ankle in dorsiflexion, the widened anterior
portion of the talus fills the mortise more effectively, improving bony stability. In plantar
flexion, the bony contribution to stability decreases, and the surrounding ligaments
must assume an increased role.6
The deltoid ligament complex stabilizes the medial aspect of the ankle. The deltoid
ligament complex is divided into two anatomically distinct layers: superficial and deep.
The superficial layer is fan-shaped and has no discrete bands. It has been divided into as
many as five components. The anatomically separate deep layer is short and thick and
divided into two distinct ligaments: the anterior and posterior tibiotalar ligaments. Both
layers act to resist valgus talar tilting and act as secondary restraints to anterior
translation of the talus. The deep layer is the primary restraint to talar external rotation.6
The lateral ankle ligament complex is configured more broadly to accommodate a wider
radius and larger arc of rotation. The lateral ankle ligament complex comprises the
anterior talofibular ligament, calcaneofibular ligament, and posterior talofibular
ligament. Lateral ankle stability depends on the orientation of the fibers of each of these
ligaments, which changes with ankle position. The anterior talofibular ligament is an
intra-articular thickening of the anterolateral ankle joint capsule. Among all lateral
ligaments, the anterior talofibular ligament has the lowest load to failure but the highest
strain, lengthening the most before failure.6
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Most ankle fractures are low-energy, rotational injuries in which the foot is planted and the
body rotates around the fixed ankle.
Ankle fractures also occur commonly during sports, usually secondary to a rotational
mechanism.
Fractures with a considerable axial loading mechanism are more severe and often result in
tibial plafond fractures.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Rotational ankle fractures represent a closed-chain injury in most patients, with the
patient’s foot contacting the ground and the body rotating around the planted foot. This
dynamic motion helps explain the incidence of these injuries in the athletic population.
Risk Factors
Cigarette smoking and increased body mass index have been associated with ankle
fractures.7,8
Associated Injuries
Common with malleolar fractures
Fractures of the talar dome occur in a substantial portion of patients with an ankle fracture
and compromise long-term outcomes.
Associated osseoligamentous injuries, such as avulsion injuries of the AITFL, may occur.
Avulsion fractures in which the AITFL avulses from the distal tibia (Chaput tubercle) or fibula
(Wagstaffe tubercle) may occur and result in associated external rotation instability.
With adduction-type ankle injuries, impaction injury to the medial distal tibia may occur.
To restore ankle joint congruency, this impaction injury may require reduction in addition to
the malleolar fracture.
This injury pattern should be considered if the medial malleolus fracture has a vertical
orientation and is associated with a transverse distal fibula fracture (Lauge-Hansen
supination adduction injury).
The lateral articular surface can be impacted in a pronation-abduction mechanism of injury.
Reduction and stabilization of the lateral articular impaction may be difficult and may result in
substantial problems with long-term outcomes because of altered bony stability and
subsequent talar tilt.

Concomitant injury to adjacent structures is common in rotational ankle fractures. This
may include partial or complete disruption of the syndesmosis, trauma to the articular
cartilage or subchondral bone of the talus, or impaction of the distal tibial articular
surface. Inferences can be made about these associated injuries in examining the
fracture pattern and/or the extent of subluxation or dislocation of the ankle joint on
injury radiographs. These injuries also can be further examined via advanced imaging
studies, such as CT or MRI.
Injury Classification
Weber/AO Foundation classification system (Figure 4)
Ankle fractures are classified based on the location of the fibular fracture.
The degree of instability depends on the location of the fibular fracture relative to the
plafond and the soft-tissue attachments that stabilize the syndesmosis.
Weber type A fracture
If the fibular fracture is located distal to the tibiofibular syndesmosis
Injury usually results from a mechanism of inversion.
Because the location is distal to syndesmosis, Weber type A fractures are unlikely to result
in instability.
Indications for surgical management are dependent on the status of the medial ankle
ligament/bone complex.
Weber type B fracture
Most common type of ankle fracture
Mechanism of injury includes an external rotation force in combination with an axial load.
Includes a fibular fracture beginning at approximately the level of the ankle syndesmosis
(the AITFL) and extending proximal and posterior
May be associated with ankle instability, depending on the status of the medial side of the
ankle
Weber type C fracture
Associated with a fibular fracture above the level of the ankle syndesmosis
Usually occurs with a mechanism of external rotation with the foot usually in a pronated
position
Generally unstable if the syndesmosis ligament complex is ruptured, and often associated
with medial injury (ligament or bone)

Lauge-Hansen classification system (Figures 5 and 6)
Ankle fractures are classified according to the mechanism of injury.
Two variables are described; the first is the position of the foot, and the second relates to
the deforming force applied to the ankle.
In a cadaver model study, most ankle fracture patterns were reproduced by placing the
foot in supination or pronation and then applying deforming forces in abduction,
adduction, or external rotation.9
If the foot is supinated, the medial deltoid ligament is relaxed, and the initial injury is
lateral.
If the foot is pronated, the deltoid ligament is tense, and the initial injury occurs medially
as a medial malleolus fracture or a deltoid ligament disruption.

The Lauge-Hansen classification describes four major fracture types: supination-adduction,
supination–external rotation, pronation–external rotation, and pronation-abduction. In
each type, the initial injury is followed by additional injury to other structures about the
ankle in a predictable sequence10 (Table 1).
Similar to the Weber classification, the Lauge-Hansen classification requires that particular
attention be paid to the specific morphology of the fibular fracture.
The Lauge-Hansen classification was first designed to aid in determining the forces
required to attain and maintain a closed reduction of an ankle fracture; however, it
continues to aid in understanding the mechanism of injury of rotational ankle fractures.
Therefore, it is useful in the surgical reduction of rotational ankle fractures before fixation.

Injury Classification
The Danis-Weber classification, commonly described as a Weber type A, type B, or type
C, is based on the level of a lateral malleolus fracture. A type A fracture is below the level
of the plafond; a type B fracture is at the level of the plafond; and a type C fracture is
above the plafond. A type A fracture without a medial fracture likely is an avulsion-type
fracture that does not lead to lateral instability of the talus and can be managed
nonsurgically. A type C fracture is inherently unstable and usually involves the
syndesmosis. The stability of a type B fracture is more difficult to determine because it
may involve a syndesmotic injury with a deltoid ligament injury (unstable) or may be a
stable injury if no medial ankle pathology is observed. A stress radiograph may help
detect medial ankle pathology if routine radiographs are normal.5
The Lauge-Hansen classification uses the position of the foot at the time of injury and
the direction of the force causing the injury to define four types of injuries: supination–
external rotation, supination-adduction, pronation–external rotation, and pronation-
abduction. Each of these types has four subtypes (I through IV) denoting injury severity.
The Lauge-Hansen system is popular but difficult to reproduce. The Lauge-Hansen
classification system is limited in making treatment decisions or providing prognostic
information; however, this system correlates the mechanism of injury with the fracture
pattern and may be useful for communicating patterns of injury and guiding closed
reduction techniques.5
Mechanics of Fractures

Mechanics of Fractures
As described in the Lauge-Hansen classification system, the mechanism of injury of
these ankle fractures is rotational, which typically results in spiral or oblique fracture
patterns of the fibula. Medial malleolus involvement generally represents more of an
avulsion-type injury and results in transverse fracture patterns perpendicular to the

attachment of the deltoid ligament. Similarly, posterior malleolus fracture fragments are
thought to represent avulsions of the posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament and usually
are vertically oriented, perpendicular to the fibers of the ligament.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical evaluation should include a description of the mechanism of injury.
An evaluation of medical comorbidities, with attention to peripheral vascular disease and
diabetes mellitus, is important. Physical examination should include a thorough inspection for
potentially communicating open wounds.
An open ankle fracture is most commonly associated with an open medial wound with a
punctate or transverse laceration in communication with the ankle joint.
These fractures should be considered surgical emergencies.
An examination for deformity of the foot relative to the leg and the direction of displacement
to the foot should be performed.
A complete circulatory and neurologic examination should be documented, including
assessment of the superficial peroneal, deep peroneal, sural, saphenous and posterior tibial
nerves, which can be examined using light touch and sharp/dull discrimination.
The condition of the skin must be considered.
Soft-tissue swelling should be assessed because it will affect surgical timing.
Fracture-dislocations should be reduced promptly to avoid isolated skin and soft-tissue
ischemia.
In patients without dislocation, the ankle should be palpated for areas of tenderness.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
A thorough circumferential examination of the ankle should be performed to evaluate
the soft tissue of the entire ankle region, including the posterior aspect. Evaluation of the
soft-tissue envelope around an ankle fracture is important because its condition may be

Patient History
A thorough patient history should pay particular attention to any medical comorbidities.
The presence of diabetes mellitus, peripheral neuropathy, or peripheral vascular disease
is important for risk stratification and decision making. The patient’s age, preinjury
activity level, occupation, and recreational activities also may be important in decision
making. Patients should be asked if osteoporosis has been diagnosed or if they have had
a fragility fracture, such as a compression fracture of the spine, a hip fracture, or a distal
radius fracture. The presence of a medical comorbidity may increase the risk of infection,
nonunion, malunion, or soft-tissue complications. A patient with obesity has an
increased risk for soft-tissue complications. A patient who uses tobacco or abuses
alcohol should be counseled about the associated fracture and wound-healing risks and
the potential advantages of cessation.5
Physical Examination
Although physical examination of acute ankle injuries is important, the ability to detect
instability via physical examination alone has been questioned.
This is particularly the true for isolated lateral malleolus fractures, in which the degree of
instability of the ankle often is difficult to determine.
In patients with an isolated fibula fracture without talar shift, the ankle should be palpated
directly over the deltoid ligament for swelling, ecchymosis, and tenderness, which indicate
potential deltoid ligament injury; however, the value of this maneuver in predicting ankle
instability is relatively limited.

indicate a Maisonneuve fracture variant with injury to the syndesmosis.5

MRI is useful for detecting ligamentous injury. Although MRI may not be economically

cartilage and dome also may be apparent on MRI and may help guide management.

visualization of critical structures on MRI, creating a false reading (positive or negative).

In general, no role for bone scintigraphy exist in patients with an acute ankle fracture;
however, it may be useful if concern for a pathologic fracture of the ankle exists.

duplex ultrasonography can be used to evaluate for deep vein thrombosis or as part the
vascular workup if clinical concern and/or risk factors for this condition exist.

Differential Diagnosis

Differential Diagnosis
In general, ankle fracture diagnosis is clear based on clinical examination and plain
radiographs. In the absence of obvious ankle fracture on plain radiographs of the ankle,
various gradations of ankle sprain, syndesmotic injury, Achilles tendon rupture, Lisfranc
or other foot fractures, and/or Maisonneuve fractures should be considered. If these
injuries have been ruled out and clinical concern for an ankle injury remains, then
advanced imaging modalities should be considered.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management remains the standard of care for ankle fractures in many patient.
In stable fibula fractures without associated medial injury, closed management leads to
excellent results in most patients.
If the fracture is stable, a short leg cast or a functional brace can be applied for 4 to 6 weeks.
Weight bearing is permitted as symptoms allow.
Prolonged immobilization and cast immobilization are not necessary.
Some studies have reported good results using a simple, supportive high-top shoe or an
elastic bandage.
Unstable fractures
With an unstable fracture, nonsurgical management requires frequent follow-up.
Radiographic confirmation that the talus has remained reduced in the mortise is required.
Cast immobilization and non–weight bearing for a minimum of 4 weeks is necessary to
prevent the ankle from displacing; however, maintenance of reduction is difficult and is

Surgical management is indicated for unstable ankle fractures.

Reduction and splinting of an ankle fracture should be performed in a timely manner.
Reduction of any dislocation or subluxation will help to alleviate pressure on the skin and
subcutaneous tissues, and proper reduction can alleviate any pressure, tethering, or
kinking of the neurovascular structures. Reduction may help to alleviate atypical joint
contact pressure that may contribute to posttraumatic arthritis. Successful reduction
typically depends on recognizing the fracture pattern and reversing the deforming force.

additional soft-tissue injury. Incorrect splinting technique may result in serious damage.
The combination of insufficient padding and the pressures added during molding may
create pressure points and lead to ulceration. Excess padding may cause the splint to be
too loose, increase shear forces, and lead to loss of reduction.5

The most common fibular fracture pattern is a Weber type B fracture with a spiral
configuration at the level of the distal tibiofibular joint. Effective fixation methods include
the use of multiple lag screws, one or more lag screws with neutralization plating, or
anti-glide plating. The plating surfaces are directly lateral or posterolateral. Laterally
based plates tend to be more prominent because this is a subcutaneous location, and
posterolateral plates may cause peroneal tendon irritation if placed too distally.5
Associated fractures also may guide the method of fibular fixation. For example, large

osteoporotic bone; however, no specific advantages of locked plates over unlocked
plates have been shown. Percutaneous fixation methods may be beneficial to protect
soft-tissue injuries because intramedullary fixation devices specific to the fibula have
been developed. The superiority of intramedullary fixation has not yet been proven in
the literature.

Posterior Malleolus
Posterior malleolus fractures involving the posterolateral corner of the distal tibia
represent avulsion of the posterior tibiofibular ligaments, which are a component of the
syndesmotic complex. Therefore, reduction and fixation of the posterior malleolus
component restores the tension and competence of the syndesmosis in this fracture
type and may provide better stability than a syndesmotic screw.5
Fixation of the posterior malleolus fragment can be achieved via several methods. For
displaced and larger fragments, a traditional posterolateral approach can be used for
direct visualization of the fragment, anatomic reduction, and application of an anti-glide
plate to facilitate compression at the fracture. Additional posterior-anterior screws can
be placed distal to the apex of the fracture to apply additional compression and stability.
An alternative technique involves percutaneous fixation with the use of cannulated
screws. This generally is reserved for smaller fragments that are minimally displaced or
nondisplaced, and fixation of these fragments may assist with syndesmotic stability.

Tibiofibular syndesmosis
Injuries to the tibiofibular syndesmosis are common with rotational ankle injuries.
Considerable controversy exists with regard to the indications for, reduction assessment of,
and methods of syndesmotic fixation.
After fixation of both malleoli, all external rotation and eversion ankle fractures should be
evaluated fluoroscopically because syndesmotic instability may be present.
Although more common in higher fibular fractures, approximately 33% to 50% of
supination–external rotation–type ankle fractures are associated with syndesmotic
instability after fibular fixation.
The syndesmosis may be stabilized with the use of one or two 3.5- or 4.5-mm screws
inserted from the fibula into the tibia. The most distal screw should be inserted at the
superior margin of the syndesmosis.
Suture-button devices are an alternative to screw fixation. Potential benefit is associated
with lack of need for removal of such flexible devices, and less precision is necessary.
Accurate, anatomic reduction of the syndesmosis is required; over-compression and
widening of the syndesmosis, malrotation, and anterior or posterior translation of the
fibula may occur.
Achieving accurate reduction is more critical if only syndesmotic fixation is performed, such
as for a proximal fibula fracture associated with interosseous membrane disruption, ankle
instability, and fibular shortening. In this instance, accurate restoration of fibular length and
alignment is required before placement of syndesmotic fixation.

Arthroscopy at the time of definitive fixation has been proposed and advocated by

direct visualization of syndesmotic instability, assessment and management of

such combined management. Overall, in the United States, 32,307 open reduction
and internal fixation procedures were performed to manage ankle fractures between
2007 and 2011. Of these procedures, 313 patients underwent simultaneous ankle
arthroscopy, representing less than 1%. Despite the purported advantages of
arthroscopy at the time of ankle fracture fixation, the long-term clinical advantages of
such management over traditional open reduction and internal fixation have yet to be
clearly delineated in the literature.17

Surgical Fracture Fixation
Fracture fixation methodology depends on the geometry and characteristics of the
various fracture patterns and generally relies on AO principles of fixation. The most
common fibular fracture pattern is a simple oblique pattern, which is amenable to
fixation with the use of an interfragmentary screw and a neutralization plate. Depending
on the location of the fracture and the quality of patient bone, a one-third tubular plate
often is adequate for neutralization. If the fracture is too distal to allow for the
placement of three screws for six cortices distal to the fracture, an anatomic plate with a
distal locking cluster can be used instead. Fibular fractures that are more highly
comminuted are amenable to bridge plating to span the zone of injury. Interest in the
development of an intramedullary fibular fracture fixation device has increased. The
advantages of this type of implant include smaller incisions, preservation of local biology
for healing, and decreased hardware profile. A prospective randomized controlled trial
found that intramedullary fibular nails provided reliable fixation with fewer soft-tissue
complications and were more cost-effective in the elderly population compared with
traditional open reduction and internal fixation.19
The most common fracture pattern of the medial malleolus is a transverse pattern, often
at the level of the talar shoulder. This pattern is amenable to interfragmentary fixation
with the use of cannulated cancellous or solid cortical screws running in a retrograde
fashion, starting at the tip of the malleolus. Some surgeons advocate for bicortical
purchase with one or more screws to provide more rigid fixation of the fracture,
especially in osteoporotic bone. A tension band construct also can be used to facilitate
compression across the fracture site. Smaller medial malleolus fragments may be
amenable to anatomic medial malleolus hook plating if screw fixation is not feasible. In
vertical medial malleolus fractures, interfragmentary screw fixation is feasible; however,
the screw trajectory is more transverse to maintain a perpendicular orientation to the
fracture line. Alternatively, an anti-glide plate can be applied. As medial malleolus
fixation is placed more posteriorly, the risk of injuring the posterior tibial tendon
increases.

Contraindications
The main contraindications to surgical fixation of an otherwise unstable ankle fracture

Surgical Fracture Fixation
Fracture fixation methodology depends on the geometry and characteristics of the
various fracture patterns and generally relies on AO principles of fixation. The most
common fibular fracture pattern is a simple oblique pattern, which is amenable to
fixation with the use of an interfragmentary screw and a neutralization plate. Depending
on the location of the fracture and the quality of patient bone, a one-third tubular plate
often is adequate for neutralization. If the fracture is too distal to allow for the
placement of three screws for six cortices distal to the fracture, an anatomic plate with a
distal locking cluster can be used instead. Fibular fractures that are more highly
comminuted are amenable to bridge plating to span the zone of injury. Interest in the
development of an intramedullary fibular fracture fixation device has increased. The
advantages of this type of implant include smaller incisions, preservation of local biology
for healing, and decreased hardware profile. A prospective randomized controlled trial
found that intramedullary fibular nails provided reliable fixation with fewer soft-tissue
complications and were more cost-effective in the elderly population compared with
traditional open reduction and internal fixation.19
The most common fracture pattern of the medial malleolus is a transverse pattern, often
at the level of the talar shoulder. This pattern is amenable to interfragmentary fixation
with the use of cannulated cancellous or solid cortical screws running in a retrograde
fashion, starting at the tip of the malleolus. Some surgeons advocate for bicortical
purchase with one or more screws to provide more rigid fixation of the fracture,
especially in osteoporotic bone. A tension band construct also can be used to facilitate
compression across the fracture site. Smaller medial malleolus fragments may be
amenable to anatomic medial malleolus hook plating if screw fixation is not feasible. In
vertical medial malleolus fractures, interfragmentary screw fixation is feasible; however,
the screw trajectory is more transverse to maintain a perpendicular orientation to the
fracture line. Alternatively, an anti-glide plate can be applied. As medial malleolus
fixation is placed more posteriorly, the risk of injuring the posterior tibial tendon
increases.

The most common complications in the management of ankle fractures involve wound
problems and infection. This occurs in 4% to 5% of patients, which underscores the
importance of careful and meticulous soft-tissue handling. Simple peri-incisional redness
and superficial tissue necrosis may be observed or managed with antibiotic agents. More
substantial wound breakdown or exposed hardware may require consultation with a
plastic surgeon. Patients with a frank wound infection or superficial infection that does
not quickly resolve should undergo surgical débridement and culture-directed antibiotic
therapy.
Malunion may have severe consequences on contact pressures in the ankle. Surgeons
should make every effort to ensure anatomic reduction during initial surgical
management because correction of malunion is more difficult after initial surgical
management. Nonunion is uncommon about the ankle but most commonly occurs in
patients with a displaced medial malleolus fracture. As previously discussed,
invagination of soft tissue and periosteum within the fracture cleft, which may
predispose patients to nonunion, is not uncommon. Any such intervening soft tissue
should be retrieved during medial malleolus fracture reduction.
Given the subcutaneous position of the fibula and the medial malleolus at the level of
the ankle, symptomatic hardware in these areas is not uncommon. Although little
literature is available to guide recommendations, hardware removal usually is delayed
until approximately 1 year postoperatively but often results in symptomatic
improvement for patients. Technical factors, such as posterolateral fibular plating,
decreasing the obliquity of screws placed in a laterally based fibular plate, and smaller
medial malleolus screws may decrease the incidence of symptomatic hardware.1
Posttraumatic arthritis is common, and treatment options include activity modifications,
bracing, distraction arthroplasty, ankle arthrodesis, and ankle arthroplasty. Management
should be tailored to the severity of the symptoms and to patient needs and

Fracture reduction has been correlated with outcomes in patients with an ankle fracture.

Several studies correlated ankle fracture outcomes with advanced patient age or the
presence of a comorbidity.29-31 A review of Medicare Part A claims from 2008 revealed a
higher rate of postoperative medical and surgical complications in patients admitted to a
nursing home after hospitalization than in other patients.29 The Nationwide Inpatient
Sample was used to review surgically managed ankle fractures in more than 140,000
patients.30 Patients with obesity and/or diabetes mellitus had more frequent in-hospital
complications and higher health-care costs than patients with neither diagnosis. The
American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database
was used to evaluate risk factors for short-term complications and hospital
readmission.31 Type I diabetes mellitus was associated with an increased risk of adverse
events, and a high American Society of Anesthesiologists classification was associated
with a high readmission rate.32
